The code is designed for the analysis of the far field patterns of antennas in the presence of perfectly conducting metal structures at UHF and above frequencies.
The code can simulate complicated structures using arbitrarily oriented flat plates, an infinite ground plane, and a finite elliptic cylinder.
The analysis is based on uniform asymptotic techniques formulated in terms of the Geometrical Theory of Diffraction (GTD).
The GTD approach is ideal for high frequency analysis as it only requires modeling the most basic structural features.
Each plate should have edges at least a wavelength long, and the cylinder's major/minor radii and length should be a wavelength in extent.
The code is structured in a modular way, with separate subroutines for computing different types of scattered fields.
Shadowing of rays is an important part of the code, with each ray path checked for shadowing by any structure.
The source can be an electric or magnetic radiator with a cosine distribution in one dimension and either a zero width or uniform distribution in the other.
The code can be interfaced with the NEC-Moment Method code to analyze complex antenna patterns.
The input data uses a command word system to minimize the amount of data that needs to be input.
The code has options to aid in debugging and testing, including printing intermediate data and isolating scattered field components.
The code has been used successfully to model aircraft shapes and can also be used for other structures like ships, trucks, and buildings.
The code is designed to be user-oriented and can be run on interactive computer systems or in batch processing.
The code is documented in two parts: a User's Manual (Part I) and a Code Manual (Part II) that describes the FORTRAN coding in detail.
The code can handle both electric and magnetic sources, and any arbitrary antenna can be simulated by superposition of elemental sources.
